model: Many educators argue that a second language is acquired more effectively when it is taught through the content of other subjects rather than as an isolated school subject. I strongly agree with this view, as integrated learning gives language a meaningful purpose and greatly increases students' exposure to it.

First and foremost, combining a language with subject content provides a real context that makes new words and structures easier to remember. When students study English only through grammar exercises, the language often feels abstract and disconnected from their lives. In contrast, when they use English to explain the water cycle, every new word is attached to a concept they need to understand. For instance, pupils in an English Program in Khon Kaen learn terms such as 'evaporation' and 'condensation' while carrying out simple experiments, so the vocabulary is reinforced by hands-on experience. As a result, the language is absorbed naturally rather than memorised and quickly forgotten.

Furthermore, integration significantly increases the time learners spend using the target language without adding extra hours to an already crowded timetable. Most Thai students receive only a few English periods each week, which is rarely enough to build fluency. If mathematics or health education is partly delivered in English, students meet the language daily in a range of situations. Admittedly, weaker students may find this approach challenging at first; however, teachers can support them with visuals, glossaries and simplified tasks. Additionally, learners tend to be more motivated because they see the language as a practical tool rather than a test subject.

In conclusion, teaching a foreign language through another subject helps students learn it more easily because it offers a meaningful context and far greater exposure. I therefore firmly believe that schools and universities should make wider use of this integrated approach.

model: It is widely observed that many students care more about the marks they receive than about the knowledge they actually gain. I strongly agree with this observation, since the education system rewards high grades above all else and students' everyday study habits clearly reflect this priority.

The primary reason for this attitude is that grades act as the key to almost every opportunity a student wants. University admission, scholarships and even first jobs are often decided by a single number on a transcript. In Thailand, for example, secondary school students know that their cumulative grade point average will affect their chances in the national university admission system, so they naturally treat each test as a gate to pass rather than a chance to learn. Many parents also judge their children's success by report cards, adding further pressure. When the stakes are this high, it is hardly surprising that students focus on the score rather than the subject.

Moreover, the way students prepare for assessments shows that learning often comes second. A common strategy is to memorise large amounts of information the night before an examination and forget most of it a week later. Some university students also choose elective courses that are easy to pass rather than ones that genuinely interest them. Admittedly, there are passionate learners who study for the joy of understanding; however, they remain a minority in a system built around rankings. Additionally, students frequently ask teachers which topics will be tested, suggesting that their effort is guided by marks rather than curiosity.

In conclusion, students place grades above genuine learning because high marks unlock future opportunities and because their study habits are shaped by examinations. For these reasons, I firmly maintain that, for most students, the grade itself has become more important than what is learned.

outline.body2: Reason 2: Teaching is a professional skill; example of an untrained foreign visitor versus a Thai TESOL lecturer; concession on pronunciation plus rebuttal (online audio); additional point on role models.

model: Many people assume that teachers who grew up speaking English are automatically more effective than those who learned it as a second language. I strongly disagree with this belief, as non-native teachers understand learners' difficulties from personal experience, and effective teaching depends on professional training rather than birthplace.

First and foremost, non-native teachers have gone through the same learning process as their students, so they can anticipate and explain common problems. A Thai English teacher, for instance, knows that Thai verbs do not change form to show past time, which is why learners often write sentences such as 'She go to school yesterday.' Having struggled with the same point herself, the teacher can explain the rule clearly and compare it with Thai. A native speaker, by contrast, may use the language perfectly but find it hard to explain why a structure is correct.

Furthermore, teaching is a professional skill that requires training, and being a native speaker is not a teaching qualification. Lesson planning, classroom management and assessment design must all be learned. In some language schools, untrained foreign visitors are hired simply because of their accent, while a Thai lecturer with a master's degree in TESOL may be overlooked. Clearly, the qualified lecturer is far more likely to help students progress. Admittedly, native speakers offer a natural model of pronunciation; however, students can now hear authentic English through podcasts, films and online videos. In addition, a successful non-native teacher is an inspiring role model who proves that fluency is achievable.

In conclusion, a teacher's first language does not determine the quality of teaching. Non-native teachers bring valuable insight into learners' problems, and professional training matters far more than nationality. I am therefore convinced that skilled non-native teachers are just as effective as their native-speaking colleagues, and often more so.

model: There is ongoing debate about whether praise and incentives or penalties are the better way to improve students' performance. I strongly agree that learners achieve more when they are rewarded than when they are punished, as rewards build lasting motivation and clearly show students what success looks like.

The most compelling reason for this view is that rewards create a positive learning environment, whereas punishment generates fear. Students afraid of being scolded or embarrassed in front of classmates tend to avoid answering questions and taking risks, both essential parts of learning. Recognition, on the other hand, encourages them to participate and keep trying. For instance, a rural primary school teacher in Khon Kaen might give stickers and public praise to pupils who finish a reading book each week. Over a term, children who once disliked reading may compete happily to read more, showing how encouragement can turn effort into a habit.

Furthermore, rewards guide behaviour more effectively because they highlight what students should do, not merely what they should avoid. Making a student stand outside the classroom for forgetting homework, for example, only removes the learner from the lesson, so he or she falls even further behind. By contrast, rewarding students who submit work on time sets a clear example for the whole class. Admittedly, schools still need clear rules; however, these rules can be maintained through positive reinforcement rather than humiliating punishment. Additionally, frequent punishment damages self-esteem, and students who feel like failures often lose interest in school altogether.

In conclusion, rewarding students is more effective than punishing them because it builds a supportive classroom atmosphere and clearly reinforces desirable behaviour. I therefore firmly believe that teachers and parents should rely on encouragement rather than penalties to help young people reach their full potential.

model: With the rapid growth of digital platforms, many people now claim that studying online is superior to attending classes in person. I strongly disagree with this claim, because face-to-face courses offer richer interaction and are essential for developing practical skills.

First and foremost, classroom learning allows immediate and meaningful interaction between teachers and students. In a physical classroom, a lecturer can notice confused faces, stop to clarify a point and adjust the pace of the lesson at once. Students can also discuss ideas with classmates, which deepens their understanding. In online courses, by contrast, many learners keep their cameras off and rarely speak, so misunderstandings remain hidden until the examination. During the COVID-19 school closures, for example, many Thai teachers found themselves teaching to a screen of black boxes with no idea whether anyone was following. Such limited communication inevitably weakens learning.

Moreover, many subjects require hands-on practice that cannot be replicated through a screen. Nursing students must learn to measure blood pressure and give injections on real equipment under close supervision, and science students need to handle laboratory instruments safely. A video may demonstrate the steps, but it cannot correct a student's hand position or build the confidence that comes from real practice. Admittedly, online courses are flexible and convenient for working adults; nevertheless, convenience is of little value if graduates lack the competence their jobs demand. Additionally, studying at home exposes learners to constant distractions, from social media to household duties.

In conclusion, face-to-face courses remain the better choice because they support genuine interaction and provide the practical training that many professions require. I therefore firmly believe that online courses should complement, rather than replace, traditional classroom teaching.

model: Some people believe that independent study is a more effective way to learn than being taught by a teacher, especially now that so much information is available online. I strongly disagree with this view, since teachers provide expert guidance and keep learners accountable.

The primary reason is that teachers offer structure and feedback that self-learners cannot easily give themselves. A person studying alone often does not know what to learn first or how topics connect, so he or she may waste time on material that is too difficult or irrelevant. More importantly, self-learners frequently cannot recognise their own mistakes. For example, someone who practises English pronunciation by copying online videos may repeat the same errors for months without realising it, whereas a teacher could identify and correct the problem in a single lesson. Expert feedback therefore prevents bad habits from becoming permanent.

Furthermore, a teacher keeps learners motivated and accountable. Studying alone requires exceptional self-discipline, and most people find it hard to continue when the material becomes difficult or when work and family responsibilities increase. Many adults, for instance, enthusiastically buy online courses but never finish them because nobody checks their progress. In a class, by contrast, regular deadlines, quizzes and a teacher's expectations encourage steady effort. It is true that the internet offers endless free resources; however, information alone is not the same as instruction, and learners still need someone to select and explain it.

In conclusion, learning with a teacher is more effective than studying alone because teachers provide clear direction, accurate feedback and the accountability that sustains effort. For these reasons, I firmly believe that most people make greater progress under a teacher's guidance than on their own.

model: Whether people should prioritise a generous income or an enjoyable job is a question that most employees face at some point. I strongly agree that a high salary is far more important than job satisfaction, as financial security is the foundation of a stable life and creates the freedom to find happiness outside work.

First and foremost, a substantial income provides the security that individuals and their families depend on. Rent, healthcare, children's education and retirement savings all require money, and no amount of enthusiasm for a job can pay these bills. In Thai society, where many adult children are expected to support their ageing parents, this responsibility is even heavier. For example, a young graduate from a rural province who must repay a student loan and send money home every month would face constant financial stress in a poorly paid but enjoyable position. A well-paid job, by contrast, allows the same person to meet these obligations with confidence.

Furthermore, a high salary creates long-term freedom, whereas job satisfaction is often temporary. Even a dream job can become routine after a few years, and a new manager or company policy can quickly destroy the enjoyment it once offered. Money, on the other hand, can be saved and invested. A well-paid employee can afford hobbies, travel and further study, so personal fulfilment can be found outside the workplace. Admittedly, an unpleasant job can be tiring; nevertheless, financial worry is usually a far greater and more lasting source of stress.

In conclusion, a generous salary matters more than job satisfaction because it guarantees security for the whole family and opens doors to a fulfilling life beyond work. I therefore firmly believe that income should be the top priority when choosing a career.

model: It is often said that the younger generation is the driving force behind social progress. I strongly agree that young people are the most effective agents of change, as they are skilled at using digital tools to mobilise others and are more willing to challenge outdated ideas.

First and foremost, young people have a remarkable ability to spread ideas and organise action through technology. Having grown up with smartphones and social media, they can design a campaign, create persuasive content and reach thousands of people within hours. For instance, when floods hit several provinces in northeastern Thailand, groups of university students quickly used online platforms to collect donations, coordinate volunteers and deliver supplies to affected villages. This speed and reach give young people a unique advantage in turning concern into real change.

Moreover, the young are generally more open-minded and less attached to existing systems. Older people may hesitate to question traditional practices because they have spent decades working within them. Young people, by contrast, are more willing to ask whether something could be done differently. This is evident in the environmental movement, where students have led campaigns to reduce single-use plastic on campuses and in local markets. Admittedly, young people often lack experience; however, they can easily seek advice from mentors, whereas fresh vision and courage are much harder to teach. In addition, the young will live longest with the consequences of today's decisions, which gives them a strong reason to act.

In conclusion, young people are society's most powerful drivers of change because they can mobilise support through technology and are willing to question the status quo. For these reasons, I firmly believe that the younger generation should be given more opportunities to lead.

model: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, some people have argued that Thailand should keep its borders closed to foreign visitors in order to protect public health. I strongly disagree with this position, as the Thai economy depends heavily on international tourism, and health risks can be managed through careful measures rather than complete closure.

The most important reason is that tourism supports the livelihoods of millions of Thai people. Hotels, restaurants, tour operators, taxi drivers, street vendors and handicraft producers all rely on spending by foreign visitors. When the borders were closed in 2020, popular destinations such as Phuket and Pattaya became almost empty, and many workers lost their jobs or returned to their home provinces with no income. From a public health perspective, this loss is also serious, because unemployment and poverty lead to poor nutrition, stress and reduced access to healthcare. Keeping the country closed would therefore harm the well-being of the very people it aims to protect.

Furthermore, health risks can be controlled without shutting the country off from the world. Measures such as vaccination requirements, health screening at airports and rapid testing allow authorities to detect and isolate cases quickly. Thailand demonstrated this approach with the Phuket Sandbox in 2021, which allowed vaccinated visitors to enter under strict conditions while the island's economy began to recover. Admittedly, reopening involves some risk; nevertheless, a well-prepared health system can respond to outbreaks far more effectively than a closed economy can recover from collapse. Additionally, international visitors promote cultural exchange and strengthen Thailand's reputation as a welcoming nation.

In conclusion, Thailand should continue to welcome international tourists because tourism sustains millions of livelihoods and modern health measures make safe travel possible. I therefore firmly believe that careful reopening, not closure, is the wiser policy.

model: Language learners often debate whether they should focus on mastering grammar rules or on developing their speaking ability. I strongly disagree with the idea that grammar study deserves more attention than conversation practice, as the main purpose of a language is communication, and speaking practice helps learners acquire grammar naturally.

First and foremost, people learn a language in order to communicate, and conversation practice develops this ability directly. Knowing grammar rules is of limited value if a learner cannot respond when someone asks a simple question. In Thailand, for example, many students study English grammar for more than ten years at school and can complete written tests accurately, yet they freeze when a foreign visitor asks them for directions. Their difficulty is not a lack of knowledge but a lack of practice in listening and responding in real time. Regular conversation builds exactly these skills, along with the confidence to use them.

Moreover, conversation practice does not ignore grammar; rather, it helps learners absorb grammatical patterns through meaningful use. When people speak, they hear correct forms repeatedly from their partners and receive immediate feedback when a message is unclear. In this way, structures such as past tense endings or question forms become automatic instead of remaining rules memorised for an examination. Children acquire the grammar of their first language in exactly this way, long before they study it formally. Admittedly, explicit grammar instruction can improve accuracy in formal writing; however, it is most effective when it supports speaking rather than replacing it.

In conclusion, practising conversation is more valuable than studying grammar because communication is the ultimate goal of language learning and speaking practice strengthens grammatical knowledge in a natural way. I therefore firmly believe that learners should spend most of their time using the language, not just analysing it.

model: Many factors contribute to national progress, including natural resources, infrastructure and political stability. Nevertheless, I strongly agree that education matters more than any of them, because it creates the skilled workforce a modern economy needs and improves the health and well-being of the whole population.

First and foremost, education produces the human capital that drives economic growth. Well-educated citizens can work in high-value industries, adopt new technologies and create innovative products instead of depending on low-wage work. Singapore and South Korea illustrate this point clearly: with few natural resources, both countries invested heavily in schools and universities and transformed themselves into prosperous, technologically advanced economies within a few decades. Natural resources, by contrast, eventually run out and cannot by themselves produce sustainable development. A nation's long-term wealth therefore lies in the knowledge and skills of its people.

Furthermore, education improves public health and quality of life, which are central to any meaningful definition of development. People with higher levels of education are better able to understand health information, prevent disease and use healthcare services appropriately. In Thailand, for instance, village health volunteers are trained to teach their neighbours about nutrition, vaccination and the control of diabetes and high blood pressure, and this community education helps reduce preventable illness. It could be argued that infrastructure and stable government matter equally; however, roads, hospitals and effective institutions all depend on educated engineers, doctors and administrators. Additionally, educated citizens are more likely to participate responsibly in public life.

In conclusion, education is the most crucial factor in a country's development because it builds a productive workforce and supports a healthier society. I therefore firmly believe that governments should make investment in education their highest priority.

outline.body2: Reason 2: Centralised testing keeps admission transparent and affordable; concession on stress and tutoring costs plus rebuttal (reform, not abolish).

model: Some critics argue that the standardised national test used for university admission should be eliminated. I strongly disagree with this proposal, since a common examination provides a fair way to compare applicants from very different schools and protects the admission process from favouritism.

The primary reason for keeping the national examination is that it offers a single, fair standard for all applicants. Schools vary greatly in quality and in their grading practices, so a high grade point average from one school may not represent the same level of knowledge as the same average from another. A national test solves this problem by asking every candidate the same questions under the same conditions. For instance, a talented student from a small rural school in Isan can demonstrate that her ability matches that of a student from a famous school in Bangkok. Without such a test, universities would have no reliable way to make this comparison.

Moreover, a centralised examination makes university admission more transparent. When results are calculated and published according to clear criteria, it becomes difficult for personal connections, donations or family status to influence who is accepted. If each university relied only on interviews, portfolios or its own tests, the process could become less open and more expensive, since students would need to travel to many campuses. Admittedly, the current examination places heavy pressure on students and encourages costly private tutoring; however, the solution is to reform the content and format of the test, not to abolish it.

In conclusion, the national university entrance examination should be retained because it ensures fair comparison between applicants and keeps admission transparent. I therefore firmly believe that improving the examination is far wiser than removing it.

outline.body2: Reason 2: Experience develops practical and interpersonal skills; example of a new lecturer learning classroom management; concession on theory from books plus rebuttal; additional point on learning from mistakes.

model: People have long debated whether knowledge gained through direct experience is more valuable than knowledge gained from reading. I strongly agree that learning by doing is superior, because experience produces deeper and longer-lasting understanding and develops practical skills that books cannot teach.

First and foremost, lessons learned through experience are remembered far longer than facts read on a page. When people actively take part in a situation, they use their senses and emotions, and they see the real consequences of their decisions. This makes the knowledge personal and meaningful. Medical education is a clear example: students may read about the symptoms of dengue fever many times, but the first time they examine a feverish child on a hospital ward and monitor the illness day by day, they understand the disease in a way no textbook can provide. Such memories remain with them throughout their careers.

Furthermore, experience develops practical and interpersonal skills that cannot be fully described in writing. Communicating with difficult people, managing time under pressure and adapting when plans fail are abilities learned mainly through practice. A newly appointed lecturer, for instance, may read several books on classroom management, yet it is the first semester of real teaching that shows how to handle a silent class or an unexpected technical failure. Admittedly, books provide useful theory and background knowledge; however, this knowledge only becomes truly useful when it is tested in real situations. Additionally, learning from mistakes builds resilience and confidence, which are essential in any profession.

In conclusion, experience is a more effective teacher than books because it creates lasting understanding and builds skills that reading alone cannot develop. For these reasons, I firmly believe that practical experience should be at the centre of education and professional training.

model: The widespread shift to online learning, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, has changed the daily lives of students. I strongly agree that this form of study has a harmful effect on learners, as it damages their physical and mental health and places a heavy social and financial burden on them and their families.

First and foremost, online learning threatens students' health. Learners who attend classes through a screen often sit in the same position for many hours a day, which can cause eye strain, back pain and a lack of physical activity. Their mental health may also suffer, since they spend long periods isolated from teachers and friends. During the school closures in Thailand, for example, some secondary students followed six or more hours of video lessons daily, leaving little time for exercise or rest. Over time, such habits may lead to long-term problems such as obesity, poor sleep and anxiety.

Moreover, online learning disrupts social development and increases pressure on families. School is not only a place for academic study; it is also where young people learn to cooperate, resolve conflicts and build friendships. Without daily face-to-face contact, these skills develop more slowly. At the same time, many families must buy devices and pay for reliable internet access. In rural parts of Isan, some parents had to borrow money to buy smartphones so that several children could attend classes simultaneously. It is true that online learning offers flexibility; nevertheless, this benefit cannot compensate for its effects on health, relationships and household finances.

In conclusion, studying online harms students' lives because it endangers their physical and mental well-being and creates social and economic difficulties. I therefore firmly believe that it should be used only as a supplement to classroom education.

model: Some people believe that individuals produce better results when they work independently rather than as part of a group. I strongly disagree with this view, because teamwork combines diverse skills to solve complex problems and allows members to share responsibilities and learn from one another.

First and foremost, a team can bring together a range of knowledge and skills that no single person possesses. Most modern problems are too complex to be solved by one individual. In healthcare, for example, a patient with diabetes is best supported by a multidisciplinary team: a doctor adjusts the medication, a nurse monitors blood sugar, a dietitian plans meals and a pharmacist checks for harmful drug interactions. Together, they provide safer and more complete care than any single professional could. The same principle applies in engineering, business and research, where combining perspectives leads to more creative and reliable solutions.

Moreover, teamwork reduces individual pressure and improves the quality of work. When tasks are divided fairly, each member can concentrate on a manageable part of the project, and colleagues can check one another's work to catch errors before they become serious. Team members also learn continuously from each other. A new lecturer who co-teaches a course with experienced colleagues, for instance, quickly gains practical ideas about assessment and student support that would take years to discover alone. Admittedly, working alone offers fewer distractions for tasks that require deep concentration; however, most workplace goals depend on cooperation. In addition, belonging to a team increases motivation and a sense of shared responsibility.

In conclusion, people generally achieve more in a team than on their own because teams combine complementary expertise and share both workload and knowledge. I therefore firmly believe that teamwork is the more effective way of working in today's complex world.

model: The rapid rise of artificial intelligence tools such as chatbots has led some people to fear that technology will damage teaching and learning. I strongly disagree with this view, as AI can provide personalised support to every learner and can free teachers to focus on the most meaningful parts of their work.

The most compelling advantage of AI is its ability to give each student individual support at any time. In a typical classroom, one teacher cannot answer every question or adjust the pace for forty learners with different needs. An AI tutor, however, can explain a concept in several ways, provide extra practice and give instant feedback on written answers. For example, a student at a small school in a rural district, where there may be no English specialist, can practise speaking with an AI conversation partner every evening and receive suggestions on vocabulary and pronunciation. In this way, AI helps narrow the gap between well-resourced and disadvantaged schools.

Furthermore, AI reduces the administrative workload that consumes much of teachers' time. Lecturers can use AI tools to draft quiz questions, summarise readings or produce initial feedback on routine assignments, and then review and improve the results. The time saved can be spent on mentoring students, leading class discussions and designing more creative lessons, which are tasks that machines cannot perform well. Admittedly, AI makes it easier for some students to submit work they did not write themselves; however, this problem can be addressed through in-class writing, oral presentations and clear guidelines on responsible use.

In conclusion, artificial intelligence will benefit education far more than it harms it, since it offers personalised learning and allows teachers to concentrate on what matters most. I therefore firmly believe that schools should embrace AI carefully rather than fear it.
